These theories are presented here without a cosmological constant or added scalar or vector potential unless specifically noted, for the simple reason that the need for one or both of these was not recognized before the [[supernova]] observations by the [[Supernova Cosmology Project]] and [[High-Z Supernova Search Team]]. How to add a [[#Cosmological constant and quintessence|cosmological constant or quintessence]] to a theory is discussed under Modern Theories (see also Einstein–Hilbert action).

=== Scalar field theories ===
{{See also|Scalar theories of gravitation}}

The scalar field theories of Nordström<ref name=Nordström1912 /><ref name=Nordström1913 /> have already been discussed. Those of Littlewood,<ref name=Littlewood1953 /> Bergman,<ref name=Bergman1956 /> Yilmaz,<ref name=Yilmaz1958 /> Whitrow and Morduch<ref name=Whitrow1960 /><ref name=Whitrow1965 /> and Page and Tupper<ref name=Page1968 /> follow the general formula give by Page and Tupper.

According to Page and Tupper,<ref name=Page1968 /> who discuss all these except Nordström,<ref name=Nordström1913 /> the general scalar field theory comes from the principle of least action:

:<math>\delta\int f \left(\tfrac{\varphi}{c^2} \right) \, ds=0</math>

where the scalar field is,

:<math>\varphi = \frac{GM} r</math>

and {{mvar|c}} may or may not depend on <math>\varphi</math>.

In Nordström,<ref name=Nordström1912 />

: <math>f(\varphi/c^2)=\exp(-\varphi/c^2), \qquad c=c_\infty</math>

In Littlewood<ref name=Littlewood1953 /> and Bergmann,<ref name=Bergman1956 />

: <math>f\left( \frac \varphi {c^2} \right) = \exp\left(-\frac{\varphi}{c^2} - \frac{(c/\varphi^2)^2} 2 \right) \qquad c=c_\infty\,</math>

In Whitrow and Morduch,<ref name=Whitrow1960 />

: <math>f\left(\frac \varphi {c^2} \right) = 1, \qquad c^2=c_\infty^2-2\varphi\,</math>

In Whitrow and Morduch,<ref name=Whitrow1965 />

: <math>f\left( \frac \varphi {c^2} \right)=\exp\left(-\frac \varphi {c^2} \right), \qquad c^2=c_\infty^2-2\varphi\,</math>

In Page and Tupper,<ref name=Page1968 />

: <math>f\left( \frac \varphi {c^2} \right) = \frac \varphi {c^2} + \alpha\left( \frac \varphi {c^2} \right)^2, \qquad \frac{c_\infty^2}{c^2} = 1+ 4 \left( \frac \varphi {c_\infty^2} \right) + (15+2\alpha) \left( \frac \varphi {c_\infty^2} \right)^2</math>

Page and Tupper<ref name=Page1968 /> matches Yilmaz's theory<ref name=Yilmaz1958 /> to second order when <math>\alpha=-7/2</math>.

The gravitational deflection of light has to be zero when ''c'' is constant. Given that variable c and zero deflection of light are both in conflict with experiment, the prospect for a successful scalar theory of gravity looks very unlikely. Further, if the parameters of a scalar theory are adjusted so that the deflection of light is correct then the gravitational redshift is likely to be wrong.

Ni<ref name=Ni1972 /> summarized some theories and also created two more. In the first, a pre-existing [[special relativity]] space-time and universal time coordinate acts with matter and non-gravitational fields to generate a scalar field.  This scalar field acts together with all the rest to generate the metric.

The action is:

: <math>S={1\over 16\pi G}\int d^4 x \sqrt{-g}L_\varphi+S_m</math>

: <math>L_\varphi=\varphi R-2g^{\mu\nu} \, \partial_\mu\varphi \, \partial_\nu\varphi</math>

Misner et al.<ref name="Misner1973">{{cite book | last1=Misner | first1=Charles W. | last2=Thorne | first2=Kip S. | last3=Wheeler | first3=John Archibald | title=Gravitation | publisher=Princeton University Press | publication-place=Princeton Oxford | date=2017-10-24 | isbn=978-0-691-17779-3 | page=}}</ref> gives this without the <math>\varphi R</math> term. <math>S_m</math> is the matter action.

: <math>\Box\varphi=4\pi T^{\mu\nu} \left [\eta_{\mu\nu}e^{-2\varphi}+ \left (e^{2\varphi}+e^{-2\varphi} \right ) \, \partial_\mu t \, \partial_\nu t \right ]</math>

{{mvar|t}} is the universal time coordinate. This theory is self-consistent and complete. But the motion of the [[Solar System]] through the universe leads to serious disagreement with experiment.

In the second theory of Ni<ref name=Ni1972 /> there are two arbitrary functions <math>f(\varphi)</math> and <math>k(\varphi)</math> that are related to the metric by:

: <math>ds^2=e^{-2f(\varphi)}dt^2-e^{2f(\varphi)} \left [dx^2+dy^2+dz^2 \right ]</math>

: <math>\eta^{\mu\nu}\partial_\mu\partial_\nu\varphi=4\pi\rho^*k(\varphi)</math>

Ni<ref name=Ni1972 /> quotes Rosen<ref name=Rosen1971 /> as having two scalar fields <math>\varphi</math> and <math>\psi</math> that are related to the metric by:

: <math>ds^2=\varphi^2 \, dt^2-\psi^2 \left [dx^2+dy^2+dz^2 \right ]</math>

In Papapetrou<ref name=Papapetrou1954a /> the gravitational part of the Lagrangian is:

:<math>L_\varphi=e^\varphi \left(\tfrac{1}{2} e^{-\varphi} \, \partial_\alpha \varphi \, \partial_\alpha\varphi + \tfrac{3}{2} e^{\varphi} \, \partial_0\varphi \, \partial_0\varphi \right )</math>

In Papapetrou<ref name=Papapetrou1954b /> there is a second scalar field <math>\chi</math>. The gravitational part of the Lagrangian is now:

: <math>L_\varphi=e^{\frac{1}{2}(3\varphi+\chi)} \left (-\tfrac{1}{2} e^{-\varphi} \, \partial_\alpha \varphi \, \partial_\alpha\varphi -e^{-\varphi} \, \partial_\alpha\varphi \, \partial_\chi\varphi + \tfrac{3}{2} e^{-\chi} \, \partial_0 \varphi \, \partial_0\varphi \right )\,</math>

=== Bimetric theories ===
{{See also|Bimetric theory}}

Bimetric theories contain both the normal tensor metric and the Minkowski metric (or a metric of constant curvature), and may contain other scalar or vector fields.

Rosen<ref name=Rosen1973>{{cite journal | last1 = Rosen | first1 = N | year = 1973 | title = A bimetric theory of gravitation | journal = General Relativity and Gravitation | volume = 4 | issue = 6| pages = 435–447 |bibcode = 1973GReGr...4..435R |doi = 10.1007/BF01215403 | s2cid = 189831561 }}</ref> (1975) developed a bimetric theory. The action is:

: <math>S={1\over 64\pi G} \int d^4 x \, \sqrt{-\eta}\eta^{\mu\nu}g^{\alpha\beta}g^{\gamma\delta} (g_{\alpha\gamma |\mu} g_{\alpha\delta |\nu} -\textstyle\frac{1}{2}g_{\alpha\beta |\mu}g_{\gamma\delta |\nu})+S_m</math>

: <math>\Box_\eta g_{\mu\nu}-g^{\alpha\beta}\eta^{\gamma\delta}g_{\mu\alpha |\gamma}g_{\nu\beta |\delta}=-16\pi G\sqrt{g/\eta}(T_{\mu\nu}-\textstyle\frac{1}{2}g_{\mu\nu} T)\,</math>

Lightman–Lee<ref name=Lightman1973 /> developed a metric theory based on the non-metric theory of Belinfante and Swihart.<ref name=Belinfante1957a /><ref name=Belinfante1957b /> The result is known as BSLL theory. Given a [[tensor field]] <math>B_{\mu\nu}\,</math>, <math>B=B_{\mu\nu}\eta^{\mu\nu}\,</math>, and two constants <math>a\,</math> and <math>f\,</math> the action is:

: <math>S={1\over 16\pi G}\int d^4 x\sqrt{-\eta}(aB^{\mu\nu|\alpha}B_{\mu\nu|\alpha} + fB_{,\alpha} B^{,\alpha}) + S_m</math>

and the stress–energy tensor comes from:

: <math>a\Box_\eta B^{\mu\nu}+f\eta^{\mu\nu}\Box_\eta B=-4\pi G\sqrt{g/\eta} \, T^{\alpha\beta} \left( \frac{\partial g_{\alpha\beta}}{\partial B_\mu\nu} \right)</math>

In Rastall,<ref name=Rastall1979 /> the metric is an algebraic function of the Minkowski metric and a [[Vector field]]. The action is:

: <math>S={1\over 16\pi G}\int d^4 x \, \sqrt{-g} F(N)K^{\mu;\nu}K_{\mu;\nu}+S_m</math>

where

: <math>F(N)=- \frac N {2+N} </math>  and  <math>N=g^{\mu\nu} K_\mu K_\nu\;</math>.

=== Quasilinear theories ===
In [[Alfred North Whitehead|Whitehead]],<ref name=Whitehead1922 /> the physical metric <math>g\;</math> is constructed (by [[John Lighton Synge|Synge]]) algebraically from the Minkowski metric <math>\eta\;</math> and matter variables, so it doesn't even have a scalar field. The construction is:

: <math>g_{\mu\nu}(x^\alpha) = \eta_{\mu\nu}-2\int_{\Sigma^-}{y_\mu^- y_\nu^-\over(w^-)^3} \left[ \sqrt{-g}\rho u^\alpha \, d\Sigma_\alpha \right]^-</math>

where the superscript (−) indicates quantities evaluated along the past <math>\eta\;</math> [[light cone]] of the field point <math>x^\alpha\;</math> and

: <math>
\begin{align}
(y^\mu)^-& =x^\mu-(x^\mu)^-, \qquad (y^\mu)^-(y_\mu)^-=0,\\[5pt]
w^- & =(y^\mu)^-(u_\mu)^-, \qquad (u_\mu) = \frac{dx^\mu}{d\sigma}, \\[5pt]
d\sigma^2 & =\eta_{\mu\nu} \, dx^\mu \, dx^\nu
\end{align}
</math>

Nevertheless, the metric construction (from a non-metric theory) using the "length contraction" [[ansatz]] is criticised.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=0704.1574|last1= Field|first1= J. H.|title= Retarded electric and magnetic fields of a moving charge: Feynman's derivation of Liénard-Wiechert potentials revisited|class= physics.class-ph|year= 2007}}</ref>

Deser and Laurent<ref name=Deser1968 /> and Bollini–Giambiagi–Tiomno<ref name=Bollini1970 /> are Linear Fixed Gauge theories. Taking an approach from quantum field theory, combine a Minkowski spacetime with the gauge invariant action of a spin-two tensor field (i.e. graviton) <math>h_{\mu\nu}\;</math> to define

: <math>g_{\mu\nu} = \eta_{\mu\nu}+h_{\mu\nu}\;</math>

The action is:

: <math>S={1\over 16\pi G} \int d^4 x\sqrt{-\eta} \left[2h_{|\nu}^{\mu\nu}h_{\mu\lambda}^{|\lambda} -2h_{|\nu}^{\mu\nu}h_{\lambda|\mu}^{\lambda}+h_{\nu|\mu}^\nu h_\lambda^{\lambda|\mu} -h^{\mu\nu|\lambda}h_{\mu\nu|\lambda} \right] + S_m\;</math>

The [[Bianchi identity]] associated with this partial gauge invariance is wrong. Linear Fixed Gauge theories seek to remedy this by breaking the gauge invariance of the gravitational action through the introduction of auxiliary gravitational fields that couple to <math>h_{\mu\nu}\;</math>.

A [[cosmological constant]] can be introduced into a quasilinear theory by changing the Minkowski background to a [[de Sitter space|de Sitter]] or [[anti-de Sitter spacetime]], as suggested by G. Temple in 1923. Temple's suggestions on how to do this were criticized by C. B. Rayner in 1955.<ref>{{cite journal|author1=Gary Gibbons|author2=Will|title=On the Multiple Deaths of Whitehead's Theory of Gravity|date=2008|pages=41–61|volume=39|issue=1|journal=Studies in History and Philosophy of Science Part B: Studies in History and Philosophy of Modern Physics|arxiv=gr-qc/0611006|doi=10.1016/j.shpsb.2007.04.004|bibcode = 2008SHPMP..39...41G |s2cid=17017857}} Cf. Ronny Desmet and [[Michel Weber]] (edited by), [https://www.academia.edu/279940/Whitehead._The_Algebra_of_Metaphysics Whitehead. The Algebra of Metaphysics]. Applied Process Metaphysics Summer Institute Memorandum, Louvain-la-Neuve, Éditions Chromatika, 2010.</ref>

=== Tensor theories ===
Einstein's general relativity is the simplest plausible theory of gravity that can be based on just one [[symmetric tensor]] field (the [[metric tensor (general relativity)|metric tensor]]).<ref>{{cite book |title=The Role of Neutrinos, Strings, Gravity, and Variable Cosmological Constant in Elementary Particle Physics |author1=Behram N. Kursunogammalu |author2=Stephan L. Mintz |author3=Arnold Perlmutter |edition=illustrated |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-306-47116-2 |page=4 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/The_Role_of_Neutrinos_Strings_Gravity_an/kZMRBwAAQBAJ}}</ref> Others include: Starobinsky (R+R^2) gravity, [[Gauss–Bonnet gravity]], [[f(R) gravity]], and [[Lovelock theory of gravity]].

==== Starobinsky ====
{{See also |Starobinsky inflation}}
Starobinsky gravity, proposed by [[Alexei Starobinsky]] has the Lagrangian
:<math>\mathcal{L}= \sqrt{-g}\left[R+\frac{R^2}{6M^2}\right]
</math>
and has been used to explain inflation, in the form of [[Starobinsky inflation]]. Here <math>M</math> is a constant.

==== Gauss–Bonnet ====
Gauss–Bonnet gravity has the action
:<math>
\mathcal{L} =\sqrt{-g}\left[R+ R^2 - 4R^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu} + R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} \right].
</math>
where the coefficients of the extra terms are chosen so that the action reduces to general relativity in 4 spacetime dimensions and the extra terms are only non-trivial when more dimensions are introduced.

==== Stelle's 4th derivative gravity ====
Stelle's 4th derivative gravity, which is a generalization of Gauss–Bonnet gravity, has the action
:<math>
\mathcal{L} =\sqrt{-g}\left[ R +f_1 R^2 + f_2 R^{\mu\nu}R_{\mu\nu} + f_3 R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma}R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} \right].
</math>

==== f(R) ====
f(R) gravity has the action
:<math>
\mathcal{L}= \sqrt{-g} f(R)
</math>
and is a family of theories, each defined by a different function of the Ricci scalar. Starobinsky gravity is actually an <math>f(R)</math> theory.

==== Infinite derivative gravity ====
[[Infinite derivative gravity]] is a covariant theory of gravity, quadratic in curvature, torsion free and parity invariant,<ref>{{Cite journal | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.031101|title = Towards Singularity- and Ghost-Free Theories of Gravity| journal=Physical Review Letters| volume=108| issue=3| article-number=031101|year = 2012|last1 = Biswas|first1 = Tirthabir| last2=Gerwick| first2=Erik| last3=Koivisto| first3=Tomi| last4=Mazumdar| first4=Anupam| bibcode=2012PhRvL.108c1101B| arxiv=1110.5249| pmid=22400725|s2cid = 5517893}}</ref>
:<math>
\mathcal{L} =\sqrt{-g} \left[ M_p^2 R + Rf_1\left( \frac \Box {M_s^2}\right)R + R^{\mu\nu}f_2 \left( \frac \Box {M_s^2} \right) R_{\mu\nu} + R^{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} f_3\left( \frac \Box {M_s^2}\right) R_{\mu\nu\rho\sigma} \right].
</math>
and 
:<math>
2f_1 \left( \frac \Box {M_s^2} \right) + f_2 \left( \frac \Box {M_s^2} \right) + 2f_3 \left( \frac \Box {M_s^2} \right) = 0,
</math>
in order to make sure that only massless spin −2 and spin −0 components propagate in the graviton propagator around Minkowski background. The action becomes non-local beyond the scale <math> M_s</math>, and recovers to general relativity in the infrared, for energies below the non-local scale <math> M_s</math>. In the ultraviolet regime, at distances and time scales below non-local scale, <math>M_s^{-1}</math>, the gravitational interaction weakens enough to resolve point-like singularity, which means Schwarzschild's singularity can be potentially resolved in [[Infinite Derivative Gravity|infinite derivative theories of gravity]].

==== Lovelock ====
Lovelock gravity has the action
:<math>
\mathcal{L}=\sqrt{-g}\ (\alpha _{0}+\alpha _{1}R+\alpha _{2}\left(
R^{2}+R_{\alpha \beta \mu \nu }R^{\alpha \beta \mu \nu }-4R_{\mu \nu }R^{\mu
\nu }\right) +\alpha _{3}\mathcal{O}(R^{3})),
</math>
and can be thought of as a generalization of general relativity.

=== Scalar–tensor theories ===
{{See also|Scalar–tensor theory|Brans–Dicke theory|Dilaton|Chameleon particle|Pressuron|Horndeski's theory}}

These all contain at least one free parameter, as opposed to general relativity which has no free parameters.

Although not normally considered a Scalar–Tensor theory of gravity, the 5 by 5 metric of [[Kaluza–Klein theory|Kaluza–Klein]] reduces to a 4 by 4 metric and a single scalar. So if the 5th element is treated as a scalar gravitational field instead of an electromagnetic field then [[Kaluza–Klein theory|Kaluza–Klein]] can be considered the progenitor of Scalar–Tensor theories of gravity. This was recognized by Thiry.<ref name=Thiry1948 />

Scalar–Tensor theories include Thiry,<ref name=Thiry1948 /> Jordan,<ref name=Jordan1955 /> Brans and Dicke,<ref name=Brans1961 /> Bergman,<ref name=Bergmann1968 /> Nordtveldt (1970), Wagoner,<ref name=Wagoner1970 /> Bekenstein<ref name=Bekenstein1977 /> and Barker.<ref name=barker1978 />

The action <math>S\;</math> is based on the integral of the Lagrangian <math>L_\varphi\;</math>.

: <math>S={1\over 16\pi G}\int d^4 x\sqrt{-g}L_\varphi+S_m\;</math>

: <math>L_\varphi=\varphi R-{\omega(\varphi)\over\varphi} g^{\mu\nu} \, \partial_\mu\varphi \, \partial_\nu\varphi + 2\varphi \lambda(\varphi)\;</math>

: <math>S_m=\int d^4 x \, \sqrt{g} \, G_N L_m\;</math>

: <math>T^{\mu\nu}\ \stackrel{\mathrm{def}}{=}\ {2\over\sqrt{g}}{\delta S_m\over\delta g_{\mu\nu}}</math>

where <math>\omega(\varphi)\;</math> is a different dimensionless function for each different scalar–tensor theory. The function <math>\lambda(\varphi)\;</math> plays the same role as the cosmological constant in general relativity. <math>G_N\;</math> is a dimensionless normalization constant that fixes the present-day value of <math>G\;</math>. An arbitrary potential can be added for the scalar.

The full version is retained in Bergman<ref name=Bergmann1968 /> and Wagoner.<ref name=Wagoner1970 /> Special cases are:

Nordtvedt,<ref name=Nordtvedt1970>{{cite journal | last1 = Nordtvedt Jr | first1 = K. | year = 1970 | title = Post-Newtonian metric for a general class of scalar–tensor gravitational theories with observational consequences | journal = The Astrophysical Journal | volume = 161 | page = 1059 | bibcode = 1970ApJ...161.1059N | doi = 10.1086/150607 | doi-access = free }}</ref> <math>\lambda=0\;</math>

Since <math>\lambda</math> was thought to be zero at the time anyway, this would not have been considered a significant difference. The role of the cosmological constant in more modern work is discussed under [[#Cosmological constant and quintessence|Cosmological constant]].

Brans–Dicke,<ref name=Brans1961 /> <math>\omega\;</math> is constant

Bekenstein<ref name=Bekenstein1977 /> variable mass theory
Starting with parameters <math>r\;</math> and <math>q\;</math>, found from a cosmological solution,
<math>\varphi=[1-qf(\varphi)]f(\varphi)^{-r}\;</math> determines function <math>f\;</math> then

: <math>\omega(\varphi)=-\textstyle\frac{3}{2}-\textstyle\frac{1}{4}f(\varphi)[(1-6q) qf(\varphi)-1] [r+(1-r) qf(\varphi)]^{-2}\;</math>

Barker<ref name=barker1978 /> constant G theory

: <math>\omega(\varphi)= \frac{4-3\varphi}{2\varphi-2} </math>

Adjustment of <math>\omega(\varphi)\;</math> allows Scalar Tensor Theories to tend to general relativity in the limit of <math>\omega\rightarrow\infty\;</math> in the current epoch. However, there could be significant differences from general relativity in the early universe.

So long as general relativity is confirmed by experiment, general Scalar–Tensor theories (including Brans–Dicke<ref name=Brans1961 />) can never be ruled out entirely, but as experiments continue to confirm general relativity more precisely and the parameters have to be fine-tuned so that the predictions more closely match those of general relativity.

The above examples are particular cases of [[Horndeski's theory]],<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Horndeski|first=Gregory Walter|date=1974-09-01|title=Second-order scalar–tensor field equations in a four-dimensional space|journal=International Journal of Theoretical Physics|language=en|volume=10|issue=6|pages=363–384|doi=10.1007/BF01807638|issn=0020-7748|bibcode=1974IJTP...10..363H|s2cid=122346086}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Deffayet|first1=C.|last2=Esposito-Farese|first2=G.|last3=Vikman|first3=A.|date=2009-04-03|title=Covariant Galileon|journal=Physical Review D|volume=79|issue=8|article-number=084003|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.79.084003|issn=1550-7998|arxiv=0901.1314|bibcode=2009PhRvD..79h4003D|s2cid=118855364}}</ref> the most general Lagrangian constructed out of the metric tensor and a scalar field leading to second order equations of motion in 4-dimensional space.  Viable theories beyond Horndeski (with higher order equations of motion) have been shown to exist.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Zumalacárregui|first1=Miguel|last2=García-Bellido|first2=Juan|date=2014-03-19 |title=Transforming gravity: from derivative couplings to matter to second-order scalar–tensor theories beyond the Horndeski Lagrangian|arxiv=1308.4685|journal=Physical Review D|volume=89|issue=6|article-number=064046|doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.89.064046|issn=1550-7998|bibcode=2014PhRvD..89f4046Z|s2cid=119201221}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Gleyzes|first1=Jérôme|last2=Langlois|first2=David|last3=Piazza|first3=Federico|last4=Vernizzi|first4=Filippo|date=2015-05-27|title=Healthy theories beyond Horndeski|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=114|issue=21|article-number=211101|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.114.211101|pmid=26066423|issn=0031-9007|bibcode=2015PhRvL.114u1101G|arxiv=1404.6495|s2cid=119117834}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Achour|first1=Jibril Ben|last2=Crisostomi|first2=Marco|last3=Koyama|first3=Kazuya|last4=Langlois|first4=David|last5=Noui|first5=Karim|last6=Tasinato|first6=Gianmassimo|date=December 2016|title=Degenerate higher order scalar–tensor theories beyond Horndeski up to cubic order|arxiv=1608.08135|journal=Journal of High Energy Physics|volume=2016|issue=12|page=100|doi=10.1007/JHEP12(2016)100|issn=1029-8479|bibcode=2016JHEP...12..100A|s2cid=59248448}}</ref>

=== Vector–tensor theories ===
Before we start, Will (2001) has said: "Many alternative metric theories developed during the 1970s and 1980s could be viewed as "straw-man" theories, invented to prove that such theories exist or to illustrate particular properties. Few of these could be regarded as well-motivated theories from the point of view, say, of field theory or particle physics. Examples are the vector–tensor theories studied by Will, Nordtvedt and Hellings."<ref name=Will1981 />

Hellings and Nordtvedt<ref name=Hellings1973 /> and Will and Nordtvedt<ref name=Will1972>{{cite journal | last1 = Will | first1 = C. M. | last2 = Nordtvedt Jr | first2 = K. | year = 1972 | title = Conservation laws and preferred frames in relativistic gravity I | journal = The Astrophysical Journal | volume = 177 | page = 757 | doi=10.1086/151754 | bibcode=1972ApJ...177..757W| doi-access = free }}</ref> are both vector–tensor theories. In addition to the metric tensor there is a timelike vector field <math>K_\mu.</math> The gravitational action is:

:<math>S=\frac{1}{16\pi G}\int d^4 x\sqrt{-g}\left [R+\omega K_\mu K^\mu R+\eta K^\mu K^\nu R_{\mu\nu}-\epsilon F_{\mu\nu}F^{\mu\nu}+\tau K_{\mu;\nu} K^{\mu;\nu} \right ]+S_m</math>

where <math>\omega, \eta, \epsilon, \tau</math> are constants and

:<math>F_{\mu\nu}=K_{\nu;\mu}-K_{\mu;\nu}.</math> (See Will<ref name=Will1981 /> for the field equations for <math>T^{\mu\nu}</math> and <math>K_\mu.</math>)

Will and Nordtvedt<ref name=Will1972 /> is a special case where

:<math>\omega=\eta=\epsilon=0; \quad \tau=1</math>

Hellings and Nordtvedt<ref name=Hellings1973 /> is a special case where

: <math>\tau=0; \quad\epsilon=1; \quad \eta=-2\omega</math>

These vector–tensor theories are semi-conservative, which means that they satisfy the laws of conservation of momentum and angular momentum but can have preferred frame effects. When <math>\omega=\eta=\epsilon=\tau=0</math> they reduce to general relativity so, so long as general relativity is confirmed by experiment, general vector–tensor theories can never be ruled out.

=== Other metric theories ===
Others metric theories have been proposed; that of [[Jacob Bekenstein|Bekenstein]]<ref name=Bekenstein2004>{{cite journal | last1 = Bekenstein | first1 = J. D. | year = 2004 | title = Revised gravitation theory for the modified Newtonian dynamics paradigm | journal = Physical Review D | volume = 70 | issue = 8| article-number = 083509 | doi=10.1103/physrevd.70.083509|arxiv = astro-ph/0403694 |bibcode = 2004PhRvD..70h3509B }}</ref> is discussed under Modern Theories.

=== Non-metric theories ===
{{See also|Einstein–Cartan theory|Cartan connection}}

Cartan's theory is particularly interesting both because it is a non-metric theory and because it is so old. The status of Cartan's theory is uncertain. Will<ref name=Will1981 /> claims that all non-metric theories are eliminated by Einstein's Equivalence Principle. Will tempers that by explaining experimental criteria for testing non-metric theories against Einstein's Equivalence Principle in his 2001 edition.<ref name=Will1981 /> Misner et al.<ref name=Misner1973 /> claims that Cartan's theory is the only non-metric theory to survive all experimental tests up to that date and Turyshev<ref name=Turyshev2006>Turyshev, S. G. (2011, September). [https://indico.ictp.it/event/a10169/session/14/contribution/10/material/0/0.pdf Solar System Tests of Relativistic Gravity]. In Workshop on Infrared Modifications of Gravity (Vol. 26, p. 30).</ref> lists Cartan's theory among the few that have survived all experimental tests up to that date. The following is a quick sketch of Cartan's theory as restated by Trautman.<ref name=Trautman1972>[[Andrzej Trautman|Trautman, A.]] (1972). [https://trautman.fuw.edu.pl/publications/Papers-in-pdf/28_01_Andrzej_Trautman.pdf On the Einstein–Cartan equations I], Bulletin de l'Academie Polonaise des Sciences 20, 185-190.</ref>

Cartan<ref name=Cartan1922 /><ref name=Cartan1923 /> suggested a simple generalization of Einstein's theory of gravitation. He proposed a model of space time with a metric tensor and a linear "connection" compatible with the metric but not necessarily symmetric. The torsion tensor of the connection is related to the density of intrinsic angular momentum. Independently of Cartan, similar ideas were put forward by Sciama, by Kibble in the years 1958 to 1966, culminating in a 1976 review by Hehl et al.

The original description is in terms of differential forms, but for the present article that is replaced by the more familiar language of tensors (risking loss of accuracy). As in general relativity, the Lagrangian is made up of a massless and a mass part. The Lagrangian for the massless part is:

:<math>
\begin{align}
L & ={1\over 32\pi G}\Omega_\nu^\mu g^{\nu\xi}x^\eta x^\zeta \varepsilon_{\xi\mu\eta\zeta} \\[5pt]
\Omega_\nu^\mu & =d \omega^\mu_\nu + \omega^\eta_\xi \\[5pt]
\nabla x^\mu & =-\omega^\mu_\nu x^\nu
\end{align}
</math>

The <math>\omega^\mu_\nu\;</math> is the linear connection. <math>\varepsilon_{\xi\mu\eta\zeta}\;</math> is the completely antisymmetric pseudo-tensor ([[Levi-Civita symbol]]) with <math>\varepsilon_{0123}=\sqrt{-g}\;</math>, and <math>g^{\nu\xi}\,</math> is the metric tensor as usual. By assuming that the linear connection is metric, it is possible to remove the unwanted freedom inherent in the non-metric theory. The stress–energy tensor is calculated from:

:<math>T^{\mu\nu}={1\over 16\pi G} (g^{\mu\nu}\eta^\xi_\eta-g^{\xi\mu}\eta^\nu_\eta-g^{\xi\nu} \eta^\mu_\eta) \Omega^\eta_\xi\;</math>

The space curvature is not Riemannian, but on a Riemannian space-time the Lagrangian would reduce to the Lagrangian of general relativity.

Some equations of the non-metric theory of Belinfante and Swihart<ref name=Belinfante1957a /><ref name=Belinfante1957b /> have already been discussed in the section on [[#Bimetric theories|bimetric theories]].

A distinctively non-metric theory is given by [[gauge theory gravity]], which replaces the metric in its field equations with a pair of gauge fields in flat spacetime.  On the one hand, the theory is quite conservative because it is substantially equivalent to Einstein–Cartan theory (or general relativity in the limit of vanishing spin), differing mostly in the nature of its global solutions.  On the other hand, it is radical because it replaces differential geometry with [[geometric algebra]].

== Modern theories 1980s to present ==
This section includes alternatives to general relativity published after the observations of galaxy rotation that led to the hypothesis of "dark matter". There is no known reliable list of comparison of these theories. Those considered here include: Bekenstein,<ref name=Bekenstein2004 /> Moffat,<ref name=Moffat1995>{{cite journal|author1=Moffat|title=Nonsymmetric Gravitational Theory|doi=10.1016/0370-2693(95)00670-G|date=1995|journal=Physics Letters B|volume=355|issue=3–4|pages=447–452|arxiv=gr-qc/9411006|bibcode = 1995PhLB..355..447M |s2cid=15879285}}</ref> Moffat,<ref name=Moffat2003>{{cite journal|author1=Moffat|title=Bimetric Gravity Theory, Varying Speed of Light and the Dimming of Supernovae|doi=10.1142/S0218271803002366|date=2003|journal=International Journal of Modern Physics D|volume=12|issue=2|pages=281–298|arxiv=gr-qc/0202012|bibcode = 2003IJMPD..12..281M |s2cid=12305911}}</ref> Moffat.<ref name=Moffat2005>{{cite journal|author1=Moffat|title=Gravitational Theory, Galaxy Rotation Curves and Cosmology without Dark Matter|doi=10.1088/1475-7516/2005/05/003|date=2005|journal=Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics|volume=2005|issue=5|page=003|arxiv=astro-ph/0412195|bibcode = 2005JCAP...05..003M |s2cid=307531}}</ref><ref name=Moffat2006>{{cite journal|author1=Moffat|title=Scalar–Tensor–Vector Gravity Theory|doi=10.1088/1475-7516/2006/03/004|date=2006|journal=Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics|volume=2006|issue=3|page=004|arxiv=gr-qc/0506021|bibcode = 2006JCAP...03..004M |s2cid=17376981}}</ref> These theories are presented with a cosmological constant or added scalar or vector potential.

=== Motivations ===
Motivations for the more recent alternatives to general relativity are almost all cosmological, associated with or replacing such constructs as "inflation", "dark matter" and "dark energy". The basic idea is that gravity agrees with general relativity at the present epoch but may have been quite different in the early universe.<ref>{{cite book |title=Differential Geometry and General Relativity: Volume 1 |author1=Canbin Liang |author2=Bin Zhou |edition= |publisher=Springer Nature |year=2023 |isbn=978-981-9900-22-0 |page=505 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Differential_Geometry_and_General_Relati/cZXTEAAAQBAJ}}</ref><ref>{{cite book |title=Phase Transitions in the Early Universe: Theory and Observations |author1=Héctor J. De Vega |author2=Isaak M. Khalatnikov |author3=Norma G. Sànchez |edition=illustrated |publisher=Springer Science & Business Media |year=2001 |isbn=978-1-4020-0056-0 |page=82 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Phase_Transitions_in_the_Early_Universe/xU56sOrFHBwC}}</ref>

In the 1980s, there was a slowly dawning realisation in the physics world that there were several problems inherent in the then-current big-bang scenario, including the [[horizon problem]] and the observation that at early times when quarks were first forming there was not enough space in the universe to contain even one quark. Inflation theory was developed to overcome these difficulties. Another alternative was constructing an alternative to general relativity in which the speed of light was higher in the early universe. The discovery of unexpected rotation curves for galaxies took everyone by surprise. Could there be more mass in the universe than we are aware of, or is the theory of gravity itself wrong? The consensus now is that the missing mass is "cold dark matter", but that consensus was only reached after trying alternatives to general relativity, and some physicists still believe that alternative models of gravity may hold the answer.{{cn|date=March 2025}}

In the 1990s, supernova surveys discovered the accelerated expansion of the universe, now usually attributed to [[dark energy]]. This led to the rapid reinstatement of Einstein's cosmological constant, and quintessence arrived as an alternative to the cosmological constant.{{cn|date=March 2025}} At least one new alternative to general relativity attempted to explain the supernova surveys' results in a completely different way. The measurement of the speed of gravity with the gravitational wave event [[GW170817]] ruled out many alternative theories of gravity as explanations for the accelerated expansion.<ref>{{cite journal |title=Challenges to Self-Acceleration in Modified Gravity from Gravitational Waves and Large-Scale Structure |journal=Physics Letters B|volume=765|pages=382–385|first1=Lucas|last1=Lombriser |first2=Nelson|last2=Lima |arxiv=1602.07670 |year=2017|doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2016.12.048|bibcode=2017PhLB..765..382L|s2cid=118486016}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://phys.org/news/2017-02-quest-riddle-einstein-theory.html|title=Quest to settle riddle over Einstein's theory may soon be over|date=February 10, 2017|access-date=October 29, 2017|website=[[phys.org]]}}</ref><ref>{{cite news|url=https://arstechnica.co.uk/science/2017/02/theoretical-battle-dark-energy-vs-modified-gravity/|title=Theoretical battle: Dark energy vs. modified gravity|date=February 25, 2017|access-date=October 27, 2017|website=[[Ars Technica]]|author=Xaq Rzetelny}}</ref> 

Another observation that sparked recent interest in alternatives to General Relativity is the [[Pioneer anomaly]]. It was quickly discovered that alternatives to general relativity could explain this anomaly. This is now believed to be accounted for by non-uniform thermal radiation.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Turyshev |first1=Slava G. |last2=Toth |first2=Viktor T. |last3=Kinsella |first3=Gary |last4=Lee |first4=Siu-Chun |last5=Lok |first5=Shing M. |last6=Ellis |first6=Jordan |title=Support for the Thermal Origin of the Pioneer Anomaly |journal=Physical Review Letters |date=2012 |volume=108 |issue=24 |article-number=241101 |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.241101 |pmid=23004253 |arxiv=1204.2507 }}</ref>

=== Cosmological constant and quintessence ===
{{See also|Cosmological constant|Einstein–Hilbert action|Quintessence (physics)}}

The cosmological constant <math>\Lambda\;</math> is a very old idea, going back to Einstein in 1917.<ref name=Einstein1917 /> The success of the Friedmann model of the universe in which <math>\Lambda=0\;</math> led to the general acceptance that it is zero, but the use of a non-zero value came back when data from supernovae indicated that the expansion of the universe is accelerating.<ref>{{cite book |title=Relativity, Gravitation and Cosmology: A Basic Introduction |author1=Ta-Pei Cheng |edition=illustrated, reprinted |publisher=OUP Oxford |year=2005 |isbn=978-0-19-852957-6 |page=185 |url=https://www.google.com/books/edition/Relativity_Gravitation_and_Cosmology/zsAiTl5hTLMC}}</ref>

In Newtonian gravity, the addition of the cosmological constant changes the Newton–Poisson equation from:

: <math>\nabla^2\varphi=4\pi\rho\ G;</math>

to

: <math>\nabla^2\varphi + \frac{1}{2}\Lambda c^2 = 4\pi\rho\ G;</math>

In general relativity, it changes the Einstein–Hilbert action from

: <math>S={1\over 16\pi G}\int R\sqrt{-g} \, d^4x \, +S_m\;</math>

to

: <math>S={1\over 16\pi G}\int (R-2\Lambda)\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x \, +S_m\;</math>

which changes the field equation from:

: <math>T^{\mu\nu}={1\over 8\pi G} \left(R^{\mu\nu}-\frac {1}{2} g^{\mu\nu} R \right)\;</math>

to:

: <math>T^{\mu\nu}={1\over 8\pi G}\left(R^{\mu\nu}-\frac {1}{2} g^{\mu\nu} R + g^{\mu\nu} \Lambda \right)\;</math>

In alternative theories of gravity, a cosmological constant can be added to the action in the same way.

More generally a scalar potential <math>\lambda(\varphi)\;</math> can be added to scalar tensor theories. This can be done in every alternative the general relativity that contains a scalar field <math>\varphi\;</math> by adding the term <math>\lambda(\varphi)\;</math> inside the Lagrangian for the gravitational part of the action, the <math>L_\varphi\;</math> part of

: <math>S={1\over 16\pi G}\int d^4x \, \sqrt{-g} \, L_\varphi+S_m\;</math>

Because <math>\lambda(\varphi)\;</math> is an arbitrary function of the scalar field rather than a constant, it can be set to give an acceleration that is large in the early universe and small at the present epoch. This is known as quintessence.

A similar method can be used in alternatives to general relativity that use vector fields, including Rastall<ref name=Rastall1979 /> and vector–tensor theories. A term proportional to

: <math>K^\mu K^\nu g_{\mu\nu}\;</math>

is added to the Lagrangian for the gravitational part of the action.

=== Farnes' theories === 
In December 2018, the astrophysicist [[Jamie Farnes]] from the [[University of Oxford]] proposed a [[dark fluid]] theory, related to notions of gravitationally repulsive negative masses that were presented earlier by [[Albert Einstein]]. The theory may help to better understand the considerable amounts of unknown dark matter and dark energy in the [[universe]].<ref name="ARX-2018">{{cite journal |last=Farnes |first=J.S. |title=A Unifying Theory of Dark Energy and Dark Matter: Negative Masses and Matter Creation within a Modified ΛCDM Framework |journal=Astronomy & Astrophysics |volume=620 |pages=A92 |arxiv=1712.07962 |year=2018 |doi=10.1051/0004-6361/201832898 |bibcode=2018A&A...620A..92F |s2cid=53600834 }}</ref>

The theory relies on the concept of [[negative mass]] and reintroduces [[Fred Hoyle]]'s creation tensor in order to allow [[matter creation]] for only negative mass particles. In this way, the negative mass particles surround galaxies and apply a pressure onto them, thereby resembling dark matter. As these hypothesised particles mutually repel one another, they push apart the Universe, thereby resembling dark energy. The creation of matter allows the density of the exotic negative mass particles to remain constant as a function of time, and so appears like a [[cosmological constant]]. Einstein's field equations are modified to:
: <math>R_{\mu \nu} - \frac{1}{2} R g_{\mu \nu} = \frac{8 \pi G}{c^4} \left( T_{\mu \nu}^{+} + T_{\mu \nu}^{-} + C_{\mu \nu} \right)</math>

Farnes' theory is a simpler alternative to the conventional LambdaCDM model, as both dark energy and dark matter (two hypotheses) are solved using a single negative mass fluid (one hypothesis). The theory should be directly testable using the [[Square Kilometre Array]] radio telescope now under construction.<ref name="Schovaers-Thesis-2019">Schovaers, C., Craeye, C., & Glineur, F. (2019). Calibration of SKA-low antenna array using drones. Ecole Polytechn. de Louvain, Université Catholique de Louvain, Ottignies-Louvain-la-Neuve, Belgium.</ref>

=== Relativistic MOND ===
{{Main|Modified Newtonian dynamics}}

The original theory of MOND by Milgrom was developed in 1983 as an alternative to "dark matter".<ref name="Milgrom papers">{{Cite journal |last=Milgrom |first=M. |date=1983 |title=A modification of the Newtonian dynamics as an alternative to the hidden mass hypothesis |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=270 |pages=365–370 |doi=10.1086/161130 |bibcode=1983ApJ...270..365M|doi-access=free }}. {{Cite journal |last=Milgrom |first=M. |date=1983 |title=A modification of the Newtonian dynamics - Implications for galaxies |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=270 |pages=371–383 |doi=10.1086/161131 |bibcode=1983ApJ...270..371M}}. {{Cite journal |last=Milgrom |first=M. |date=1983 |title=A modification of the Newtonian dynamics - Implications for galaxy systems |journal=Astrophysical Journal |volume=270 |pages= 384–389|doi= 10.1086/161132 |bibcode=1983ApJ...270..384M}}.</ref> Departures from Newton's law of gravitation are governed by an acceleration scale, not a distance scale. MOND has made a number of successful, "prior" predictions, that is, predictions of unknown facts that were subsequently confirmed by observation.<ref name="merritt">{{cite book | last=Merritt | first=David | title=A Philosophical Approach to MOND: Assessing the Milgromian Research Program in Cosmology | publisher=Cambridge University Press | publication-place=Cambridge, UK | date=2020 | isbn=978-1-108-61092-6 | page=}}</ref>{{rp|p=ix}}. For example, Milgrom predicted in 1993 that the baryonic mass of a galaxy scales as the fourth power of the flat rotation speed and this was subsequently confirmed by observation.<ref name="BTFR">{{cite journal |last1=McGaugh |first1=S. S. |last2=Schombert |first2=J. M. |last3=Bothun |first3=G. D. |last4=de Blok|first4=W. J. G.|year=2000 |title=The baryonic Tully-Fisher relation. |journal=The Astrophysical Journal Letters|volume=533 |page=L99 |arxiv=1112.3960 |bibcode=2000ApJ...533L..99M |doi=10.1086/312628 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

Many attempts at a relativistic version of MOND exist, as reviewed by Famaey and McGaugh.<ref name="famaey mcgaugh">{{cite journal |last1=Famaey |first1=B. |last2=McGaugh |first2=S. |year=2012 |title=Modified Newtonian dynamics (MOND): Observational phenomenology and relativistic extensions |journal=Living Reviews in Relativity |volume=15 |issue=1 |page=10 |arxiv=1112.3960 |bibcode=2012LRR....15...10F |doi=10.12942/lrr-2012-10 |pmc=5255531 |pmid=28163623 |doi-access=free}}</ref> In so far as these theories actually reduce to non-relativistic MOND in the weak field limit they inherit its apparent failure to reproduce the correct gravitational potentials of galaxy clusters.<ref name="Aguirre">{{cite journal |author=Anthony Aguirre |author2=Joop Schaye |author3=Eliot Quataert |name-list-style=amp |date=2001 |title=Problems for Modified Newtonian Dynamics in Clusters and the Lyα Forest? |journal=The Astrophysical Journal |volume=561 |issue=2 |pages=550–558 |arxiv=astro-ph/0105184 |bibcode=2001ApJ...561..550A |doi=10.1086/323376 |s2cid=119071058}}</ref>

RAQUAL, the relativistic version of MOND's field equation [[AQUAL]] has a three part action:<ref name="aqual">{{cite journal |author=Jacob Bekenstein |author2=M. Milgrom |name-list-style=amp |date=1984 |title=Does the missing mass problem signal the breakdown of Newtonian gravity? |journal=Astrophys. J. |volume=286 |pages=7–14 |bibcode=1984ApJ...286....7B |doi=10.1086/162570}}</ref>{{rp|p=13}}

: <math>S=S_g+S_s+S_m</math>

: <math>S_g={c^4 \over 16 \pi G}\int e^{-2\phi^2} \left[ R(\tilde g_{\mu\nu}) + \dfrac{6}{c^4}\phi_{,\alpha}\phi_{,}^{\alpha} \right] \sqrt{-g}\,d^4x</math>

: <math>S_{\phi}=\dfrac{-a_0^2\beta(1+\beta)^2}{8 \pi G}\int e^{-4\phi^2} f \left[ \dfrac{e^{-2\phi^2}\phi_{,\mu}\phi_{,}^{\mu}}{a_0^2(1+\beta^2)} \right] \sqrt{-g}\,d^4x </math>

with a standard mass action. Here <math>f</math> is an arbitrary function selected to give Newtonian and MOND behaviour in the correct limits. In the strong field limit this becomes a Brans-Dicke scalar-tensor theory with <math>\beta=2\omega +3</math>. This theory was soon rejected because it allowed waves in the scalar field to propagate faster than light.<ref name=merritt/> By 1988, a second scalar field (PCC) fixed problems with this earlier scalar–tensor version but is in conflict with the perihelion precession of Mercury and gravitational lensing by galaxies and clusters. By 1997, MOND had been successfully incorporated in a stratified relativistic theory [Sanders], but as this is a [[preferred frame]] theory it has problems of its own. Despite these problems core concepts of RAQUAL such as a weak field limit that follows <math>f(\chi)\approx\chi^\frac{3}{2}</math> have been adopted under the name "[[Extended theories of gravity|extended gravity]]". [[Jacob Bekenstein]] developed a relativistic generalization of MOND in 2004, [[TeVeS]], which however had its own set of problems (see below). An attempt by Skordis and Złośnik in 2021 has been claimed to be compatible with cosmic microwave background observations, but appears to be highly contrived.<ref name="physicsworld">{{cite web|url=https://physicsworld.com/a/cosmic-combat-delving-into-the-battle-between-dark-matter-and-modified-gravity|title=Cosmic combat: delving into the battle between dark matter and modified gravity|date=6 February 2024|author=Keith Cooper|publisher=physicsworld}}</ref><ref name="skordis_zlosnik_aest">{{cite journal | last1=Skordis | first1=Constantinos | last2=Złośnik | first2=Tom | title=New Relativistic Theory for Modified Newtonian Dynamics | journal=Physical Review Letters | volume=127 | issue=16 | date=2021-10-15 | issn=0031-9007 | doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.127.161302 | doi-access=free | article-number=161302| pmid=34723619 | arxiv=2007.00082 | bibcode=2021PhRvL.127p1302S }}</ref>

==== TeVeS ====
{{Main|Tensor–vector–scalar gravity}}

Bekenstein<ref name=Bekenstein2004 /> introduced a [[tensor–vector–scalar gravity|tensor–vector–scalar]] model (TeVeS) that attempted to reproduce MOND in 2004. This has two scalar fields <math>\varphi</math>  and <math>\sigma\;</math> and vector field <math>U_\alpha</math>. The action is split into parts for gravity, scalars, vector and mass.

: <math>S=S_g+S_s+S_v+S_m</math>

The gravity part is the same as in general relativity.

:<math>\begin{align}
S_s &= -\frac{1}{2}\int \left [\sigma^2 h^{\alpha\beta}\varphi_{,\alpha}\varphi_{,\beta} + \frac12G \ell_0^{-2}\sigma^4F(kG\sigma^2)\right ]\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x \\[5pt]
S_v &= -\frac{K}{32\pi G}\int \left [g^{\alpha\beta}g^{\mu\nu}U_{[\alpha,\mu]}U_{[\beta,\nu]} -\frac{2\lambda}{K} \left (g^{\mu\nu} U_\mu U_\nu+1 \right ) \right ]\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x \\[5pt]
S_m &= \int L \left (\tilde g_{\mu\nu},f^\alpha,f^\alpha_{|\mu},\ldots \right)\sqrt{-g}\,d^4x
\end{align}</math>

where

:<math>h^{\alpha\beta} = g^{\alpha\beta}-U^\alpha U^\beta</math>
:<math>\tilde g^{\alpha\beta}=e^{2\varphi}g^{\alpha\beta}+2U^\alpha U^\beta\sinh(2\varphi)</math>

<math>k, K</math> are constants, square brackets in indices <math>U_{[\alpha,\mu]}</math> represent anti-symmetrization, <math>\lambda</math> is a Lagrange multiplier (calculated elsewhere), and {{mvar|L}} is a Lagrangian translated from flat spacetime onto the metric <math>\tilde g^{\alpha\beta}</math>. Note that {{mvar|G}} need not equal the observed gravitational constant <math>G_{Newton}</math>. {{mvar|F}} is an arbitrary function, and

:<math>F(\mu)=\frac{3}{4}{\mu^2(\mu-2)^2\over 1-\mu}</math>

is given as an example with the right asymptotic behaviour; note how it becomes undefined when <math>\mu=1</math>

The Parametric post-Newtonian parameters of this theory are calculated in,<ref>{{cite journal|last=Sagi|first=Eva|title=Preferred frame parameters in the tensor–vector–scalar theory of gravity and its generalization|journal=Physical Review D|volume=80|issue=4|article-number=044032|date=July 2009|arxiv=0905.4001|bibcode = 2009PhRvD..80d4032S |doi = 10.1103/PhysRevD.80.044032 |s2cid=118854650}}</ref> which shows that all its parameters are equal to general relativity's, except for

:<math>\begin{align}
\alpha_1 &= \frac{4G}{K} \left ((2K-1) e^{-4\varphi_0} - e^{4\varphi_0} + 8 \right ) - 8 \\[5pt]
\alpha_2 &= \frac{6 G}{2 - K} - \frac{2 G (K + 4) e^{4 \varphi_0}}{(2 - K)^2} - 1
\end{align}</math>

both of which expressed in [[geometric units]] where <math>c = G_{Newtonian} = 1</math>; so

:<math> G^{-1} = \frac{2}{2-K} + \frac{k}{4\pi}.</math>

TeVeS faces problems when confronted with data on the [[anisotropy]] of the [[cosmic microwave background]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Slosar |first1=Anže|author2-link=Alessandro Melchiorri |last2=Melchiorri |first2=Alessandro |last3=Silk |first3=Joseph I. |year=2005 |title=Test of modified Newtonian dynamics with recent Boomerang data |journal=Physical Review D |volume=72 |issue=10 |article-number=101301 |arxiv=astro-ph/0508048 |bibcode=2005PhRvD..72j1301S |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.72.101301}}</ref> the lifetime of compact objects,<ref name="Seifert2007">{{cite journal |last1=Seifert |first1=M. D. |date=2007 |title=Stability of spherically symmetric solutions in modified theories of gravity |journal=[[Physical Review D]] |volume=76 |issue=6 |article-number=064002 |arxiv=gr-qc/0703060 |bibcode=2007PhRvD..76f4002S |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.76.064002 |s2cid=29014948}}</ref> and the relationship between the lensing and matter overdensity potentials.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Zhang |first1=P. |last2=Liguori |first2=M. |last3=Bean |first3=R. |last4=Dodelson |first4=S. |date=2007 |title=Probing Gravity at Cosmological Scales by Measurements which Test the Relationship between Gravitational Lensing and Matter Overdensity |journal=[[Physical Review Letters]] |volume=99 |issue=14 |article-number=141302 |arxiv=0704.1932 |bibcode=2007PhRvL..99n1302Z |doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.99.141302 |pmid=17930657 |s2cid=119672184}}</ref> TeVeS also appears inconsistent with the speed of gravitational waves according to LIGO.<ref name="GW170817">{{citation |last1=Boran |first1=Sibel |title=GW170817 Falsifies Dark Matter Emulators |journal=Physical Review D |volume=97 |issue=4 |article-number=041501 |year=2018 |arxiv=1710.06168 |bibcode=2018PhRvD..97d1501B |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.97.041501 |s2cid=119468128 |last2=Desai |first2=Shantanu |last3=Kahya |first3=Emre |last4=Woodard |first4=Richard}}</ref>

=== Moffat's theories ===
[[J. W. Moffat]]<ref name=Moffat1995 /> developed a [[Nonsymmetric gravitational theory|non-symmetric gravitation theory]]. This is not a metric theory. It was first claimed that it does not contain a black hole horizon, but Burko and Ori<ref name=Burko1995>{{cite journal | last1 = Burko | first1 = L.M. | last2 = Ori | first2 = A. | year = 1995 | title = On the Formation of Black Holes in Nonsymmetric Gravity | journal = Physical Review Letters | volume = 75 | issue = 13| pages = 2455–2459 | doi=10.1103/physrevlett.75.2455| pmid = 10059316 |arxiv = gr-qc/9506033 |bibcode = 1995PhRvL..75.2455B | s2cid = 16615589 }}</ref> have found that nonsymmetric gravitational theory can contain black holes. Later, Moffat claimed that it has also been applied to explain rotation curves of galaxies without invoking "dark matter". Damour, Deser & McCarthy<ref name=Damour1993>{{cite book|arxiv=gr-qc/9312030|author1=Damour|author2=Deser|author3=McCarthy|title=Nonsymmetric Gravity has Unacceptable Global Asymptotics|url=https://archive.org/details/arxiv-gr-qc9312030|date=1993|bibcode=1993nghu.book.....D}}</ref> have criticised nonsymmetric gravitational theory, saying that it has unacceptable asymptotic behaviour.

The mathematics is not difficult but is intertwined so the following is only a brief sketch. Starting with a non-symmetric tensor <math>g_{\mu\nu}\;</math>, the Lagrangian density is split into

: <math>L=L_R+L_M\;</math>

where <math>L_M\;</math> is the same as for matter in general relativity.

: <math>L_R = \sqrt{-g} \left[R(W)-2\lambda-\frac14\mu^2g^{\mu\nu}g_{[\mu\nu]}\right] - \frac16g^{\mu\nu}W_\mu W_\nu\;</math>

where <math>R(W)\;</math> is a curvature term analogous to but not equal to the Ricci curvature in general relativity, <math>\lambda\;</math> and <math>\mu^2\;</math> are cosmological constants, <math>g_{[\nu\mu]}\;</math> is the antisymmetric part of <math>g_{\nu\mu}\;</math>.
<math>W_\mu\;</math> is a connection, and is a bit difficult to explain because it's defined recursively. However, <math>W_\mu\approx-2g^{,\nu}_{[\mu\nu]}\;</math>

Haugan and Kauffmann<ref name=Haugan1996>{{cite journal | last1 = Haugan | first1 = Mark | last2 = Kauffmann | first2 = Thierry | year = 1996 | title = New test of the Einstein equivalence principle and the isotropy of space | journal = Physical Review D | volume = 52 | issue = 6 | pages = 3168–3175 | doi=10.1103/physrevd.52.3168| pmid = 10019545 |arxiv = gr-qc/9504032 |bibcode = 1995PhRvD..52.3168H | s2cid = 14791921 }}</ref> used polarization measurements of the light emitted by galaxies to impose sharp constraints on the magnitude of some of nonsymmetric gravitational theory's parameters. They also used Hughes-Drever experiments to constrain the remaining degrees of freedom. Their constraint is eight orders of magnitude sharper than previous estimates.

Moffat's<ref name=Moffat2005 /> [[metric-skew-tensor-gravity]] (MSTG) theory is able to predict rotation curves for galaxies without either dark matter or MOND, and claims that it can also explain gravitational lensing of galaxy clusters without dark matter. It has variable <math>G\;</math>, increasing to a final constant value about a million years after the big bang.
 
The theory seems to contain an asymmetric tensor <math>A_{\mu\nu}\;</math> field and a source current <math>J_\mu\;</math> vector. The action is split into:

: <math>S=S_G+S_F+S_{FM}+S_M\;</math>

Both the gravity and mass terms match those of general relativity with cosmological constant. The skew field action and the skew field matter coupling are:

: <math>S_F=\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g} \left( \frac1{12}F_{\mu\nu\rho}F^{\mu\nu\rho} - \frac14\mu^2 A_{\mu\nu}A^{\mu\nu} \right)\;</math>

: <math>S_{FM}=\int d^4x\,\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\mu\nu}A_{\alpha\beta}\partial_\mu J_\nu\;</math>

where

: <math>F_{\mu\nu\rho}=\partial_\mu A_{\nu\rho}+\partial_\rho A_{\mu\nu}</math>

and <math>\epsilon^{\alpha\beta\mu\nu}\;</math> is the [[Levi-Civita symbol]]. The skew field coupling is a Pauli coupling and is gauge invariant for any source current. The source current looks like a matter fermion field associated with [[baryon number|baryon]] and [[lepton number]].

==== Scalar–tensor–vector gravity ====
{{Main|Scalar–tensor–vector gravity}}

Moffat's [[Scalar–tensor–vector gravity]]<ref name=Moffat2006 /> contains a tensor, vector and three scalar fields. But the equations are quite straightforward. The action is split into: <math> S=S_G+S_K+S_S+S_M</math> with terms for gravity, vector field <math>K_\mu,</math> scalar fields <math>G, \omega, \mu</math> and mass. <math>S_G</math> is the standard gravity term with the exception that <math>G</math> is moved inside the integral.

: <math>S_K=-\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g}\omega \left( \frac14 B_{\mu\nu} B^{\mu\nu} + V(K) \right), \qquad \text{where } \quad B_{\mu\nu}=\partial_\mu K_\nu-\partial_\nu K_\mu.</math>

: <math>S_S = -\int d^4x\,\sqrt{-g} \frac{1}{G^3} \left( \frac12g^{\mu\nu}\,\nabla_\mu G\,\nabla_\nu G -V(G) \right) + \frac{1}{G} \left( \frac{1}{2} g^{\mu\nu}\,\nabla_\mu\omega\,\nabla_\nu\omega -V(\omega) \right) +{1\over\mu^2G} \left( \frac12g^{\mu\nu}\,\nabla_\mu\mu\,\nabla_\nu\mu - V(\mu) \right).</math>

The potential function for the vector field is chosen to be:

: <math>V(K) = -\frac12\mu^2\varphi^\mu\varphi_\mu - \frac14g \left (\varphi^\mu \varphi_\mu \right )^2</math>

where <math>g</math> is a coupling constant. The functions assumed for the scalar potentials are not stated.

=== Infinite derivative gravity ===
{{Main|Infinite derivative gravity}}
In order to remove ghosts in the modified propagator, as well as to obtain asymptotic freedom, Biswas, [[Anupam Mazumdar|Mazumdar]] and [[Warren Siegel|Siegel]] (2005) considered a string-inspired infinite set of higher derivative terms
:<math>S = \int \mathrm{d}^4x  \sqrt{-g} \left(\frac{R}{2} + R F (\Box) R \right)</math>
where <math> F (\Box)</math> is the exponential of an entire function of the [[d'Alembert operator|D'Alembertian operator]].<ref>{{cite journal|title=Bouncing Universes in String-inspired Gravity|journal=Journal of Cosmology and Astroparticle Physics|volume=2006|issue=3|page=009|arxiv=hep-th/0508194|bibcode = 2006JCAP...03..009B |doi = 10.1088/1475-7516/2006/03/009 |year=2006|last1=Biswas|first1=Tirthabir|last2=Mazumdar|first2=Anupam|last3=Siegel|first3=Warren|s2cid=7445076}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|arxiv=1308.2319 |title=Generalized ghost-free quadratic curvature gravity|journal=Classical and Quantum Gravity|volume=31|issue=1|article-number=015022|last1=Biswas|first1=Tirthabir|last2=Conroy|first2=Aindriú|last3= Koshelev|first3=Alexey S.|last4=Mazumdar|first4=Anupam|year=2013|doi=10.1088/0264-9381/31/1/015022|bibcode = 2014CQGra..31a5022B |s2cid=119103482}}</ref> This avoids a black hole singularity near the origin, while recovering the 1/r fall of the general relativity potential at large distances.<ref>{{Cite journal|arxiv=1110.5249|title=Towards singularity and ghost free theories of gravity|journal=Physical Review Letters|volume=108|issue=3|last1=Biswas|first1=Tirthabir|last2=Gerwick|first2=Erik|last3=Koivisto|first3=Tomi|last4=Mazumdar|first4=Anupam|year=2011|doi=10.1103/PhysRevLett.108.031101|bibcode=2012PhRvL.108c1101B|pmid=22400725|article-number=031101|s2cid=5517893}}</ref> [[Carlos Lousto|Lousto]] and Mazzitelli (1997) found an exact solution to this theories representing a gravitational shock-wave.<ref>{{cite journal |doi=10.1103/PhysRevD.56.3471|title=Exact self-consistent gravitational shock wave in semiclassical gravity|journal=Physical Review D|volume=56|issue=6|pages=3471–3477|year=1997|last1=Lousto|first1=Carlos O|last2=Mazzitelli|first2=Francisco D|bibcode=1997PhRvD..56.3471L|arxiv=gr-qc/9611009|s2cid=5075915}}</ref>

=== General relativity self-interaction (GRSI) ===
The General Relativity Self-interaction or '''GRSI model'''<ref>{{cite journal |title=Review of latest advances on dark matter from the viewpoint of the Occam razor principle |author=Oks, Eugene |journal=New Astronomy Reviews |volume=96 |year=2023 |article-number=101673 |issn=1387-6473 |doi=10.1016/j.newar.2023.101673 |bibcode=2023NewAR..9601673O |s2cid=256262366 }}</ref> is an attempt to explain astrophysical and cosmological observations without [[dark matter]], [[dark energy]] by adding [[Nonlinear system|self-interaction]] terms when calculating the gravitational effects in [[general relativity]], analogous to the self-interaction terms in [[quantum chromodynamics]].<ref name="Deur19a">{{cite journal |arxiv=1709.02481|doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-019-7393-0|doi-access=free|title=An explanation for dark matter and dark energy consistent with the Standard Model of particle physics and General Relativity|year=2019|last1=Deur|first1=Alexandre|journal=Eur. Phys. J. C|volume=79 |issue=10|article-number=883|bibcode=2019EPJC...79..883D |s2cid=119218121 }}</ref>
Additionally, the model explains the [[Tully-Fisher relation]],<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Deur |first=A. |date=June 2009 |title=Implications of graviton–graviton interaction to dark matter |url=https://linkinghub.elsevier.com/retrieve/pii/S0370269309004870 |journal=Physics Letters B |language=en |volume=676 |issue=1–3 |pages=21–24 |doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2009.04.060|arxiv=0901.4005 |bibcode=2009PhLB..676...21D }}</ref>
the [[Galaxy rotation curve#Alternatives to dark matter|radial acceleration relation]],<ref>{{cite journal |title=Significance of Gravitational Nonlinearities on the Dynamics of Disk Galaxies |author=Deur, A.; Sargent, C.; Terzić, B. |journal=Astrophys. J. |volume=896 |issue=2 |year=2020 |page=94 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/ab94b6 |arxiv=1909.00095 |bibcode=2020ApJ...896...94D |doi-access=free }}</ref> observations that are currently challenging to understand within [[Lambda-CDM]].

The model was proposed in a series of articles, the first dating from 2003.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=astro-ph/0309474 |title=Non-Abelian Effects in Gravitation |year=2003 |last1=Deur |first1=Alexandre }}</ref> The basic point is that since within General Relativity, gravitational fields couple to each other, this can effectively increase the gravitational interaction between massive objects. The additional gravitational strength then avoid the need for dark matter. This field coupling is the origin of General Relativity's [[Nonlinear system|non-linear]] behavior. It can be understood, in particle language, as [[gravitons]] interacting with each other (despite being [[Massless particle|massless]]) because they carry [[Four-momentum|energy-momentum]].

A natural implication of this model is its explanation of the [[accelerating expansion of the universe]] without resorting to [[dark energy]].<ref name="Deur19a">{{cite journal |arxiv=1709.02481|doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-019-7393-0|doi-access=free|title=An explanation for dark matter and dark energy consistent with the Standard Model of particle physics and General Relativity|year=2019|last1=Deur|first1=Alexandre|journal=Eur. Phys. J. C|volume=79 |issue=10|article-number=883|bibcode=2019EPJC...79..883D |s2cid=119218121 }}</ref> The increased [[binding energy]] within a galaxy requires, by [[energy conservation]], a weakening of gravitational attraction outside said galaxy. This mimics the repulsion of dark energy.

The GRSI model is inspired from the [[Strong interaction|Strong Nuclear Force]], where a comparable phenomenon occurs. The interaction between [[gluons]] emitted by static or nearly static [[quarks]] dramatically strengthens quark-quark interaction, ultimately leading to [[Color confinement|quark confinement]] on the one hand (analogous to the need of stronger gravity to explain away dark matter) and the [[Nuclear force|suppression of the Strong Nuclear Force outside hadrons]] (analogous to the repulsion of dark energy that balances gravitational attraction at large scales.) Two other parallel phenomena are the [[Tully-Fisher relation]] in galaxy dynamics that is analogous to the [[Regge theory|Regge trajectories]] emerging from the strong force. In both cases, the phenomenological formulas describing these observations are similar, albeit with different numerical factors.

These parallels are expected from a theoretical point of view: General Relativity and the Strong Interaction [[Lagrangian mechanics|Lagrangians]] have the same form.<ref name="zee">{{cite book | last=Zee | first=A. | title=Quantum Field Theory in a Nutshell | publisher=Princeton University Press | publication-place=Princeton, N.J | date=2010-02-21 | isbn=978-0-691-14034-6 | oclc=318585662 | page=}}</ref><ref name="Deur09" /> The validity of the GRSI model then simply hinges on whether the coupling of the gravitational fields is large enough so that the same effects that occur in [[hadrons]] also occur in very massive systems. This coupling is effectively given by <math>\sqrt{GM/L}</math>, where <math>G</math> is the [[gravitational constant]], <math>M</math> is the mass of the system, and <math>L</math> is a characteristic length of the system. The claim of the GRSI proponents, based either on [[Lattice gauge theory|lattice calculations]],<ref name="Deur09" /> a background-field model.<ref  name="Deur21a" /> or the coincidental phenomenologies in galactic or hadronic dynamics mentioned in the previous paragraph, is that <math>\sqrt{GM/L}</math> is indeed sufficiently large for large systems such as galaxies.

====List of topics studied in the Model====
The main observations that appear to require dark matter and/or dark energy can be explained within this model. Namely,

* The [[Galaxy rotation curve|flat rotation curves of galaxies]].<ref name="Deur09">{{cite journal |arxiv=0901.4005|title=Implications of Graviton-Graviton Interaction to Dark Matter|year=2009|last1=Deur|first1=Alexandre|journal=Phys. Lett. B|volume=676 |issue=1–3|pages=21–24|doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2009.04.060 |bibcode=2009PhLB..676...21D |s2cid=118596512 }}</ref><ref name="Deur21a">{{cite journal |arxiv=2004.05905|doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-021-08965-5|doi-access=free|title=Relativistic corrections to the rotation curves of disk galaxies|year=2021|last1=Deur|first1=Alexandre|journal=Eur. Phys. J. C|volume=81 |issue=3|article-number=213|bibcode=2021EPJC...81..213D |s2cid=215745418 }}</ref><ref name="Deur16a" >{{cite journal |title=Self-interacting scalar fields at high-temperature |author=Deur, A. |journal=Eur. Phys. J. C |volume=77 |issue=6 |year=2017 |article-number=412 |doi=10.1140/epjc/s10052-017-4971-x  |doi-access=free|arxiv=1611.05515|bibcode=2017EPJC...77..412D |s2cid=254106132 }}</ref> These results, however, have been challenged.<ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=2303.11094 |title=Does gravitational confinement sustain flat galactic rotation curves without dark matter? |year=2023 |last1=Barker |first1=W. E. V. |last2=Hobson |first2=M. P. |last3=Lasenby |first3=A. N.|class=gr-qc }}</ref><ref>{{cite arXiv |eprint=2306.00992 |title=Comment on "Does gravitational confinement sustain flat galactic rotation curves without dark matter?" |year=2023 |last1=Deur |first1=A.|class=gr-qc }}</ref>
* The [[Cosmic Microwave Background]] [[anisotropies]].<ref name="Deur22a">{{cite journal |title=Effect of the field self-interaction of General Relativity on the cosmic microwave background anisotropies |author=Deur, A. |journal=Class. Quant. Grav. |volume=39 |issue=13 |year=2022 |page=135003 |doi=10.1088/1361-6382/ac7029 |arxiv=2203.02350|bibcode=2022CQGra..39m5003D |s2cid=247244759 }}</ref>
* The [[Accelerating expansion of the universe#Supernova observation|fainter luminosities of distant supernovae]] and their consequence on the [[accelerating expansion of the universe]].<ref name="Deur19a" />
* The [[Structure formation|formation of the Universe's large structures]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Effect of gravitational field self-interaction on large structure formation |author=Deur, A. |journal=Phys. Lett. B |volume=820 |year=2021 |article-number=136510 |doi=10.1016/j.physletb.2021.136510 |arxiv=2108.04649|bibcode=2021PhLB..82036510D |s2cid=236965796 }}</ref>
* The [[matter power spectrum]].<ref name="Deur22a" />
* The internal dynamics of [[galaxy clusters]], including that of the [[Bullet Cluster]].<ref name="Deur09" />

Additionally, the model explains observations that are currently challenging to understand within [[Lambda-CDM]]:

* The [[Tully-Fisher relation]].<ref name="Deur09" /><ref  name="Deur21a" />
* The [[Galaxy rotation curve#Alternatives to dark matter|radial acceleration relation]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Significance of Gravitational Nonlinearities on the Dynamics of Disk Galaxies |author=Deur, A.; Sargent, C.; Terzić, B. |journal=Astrophys. J. |volume=896 |issue=2 |year=2020 |page=94 |doi=10.3847/1538-4357/ab94b6 |arxiv=1909.00095 |bibcode=2020ApJ...896...94D |doi-access=free }}</ref>
* The [[Hubble's law#Hubble tension|Hubble tension]].<ref>{{cite journal |title=Hubble tension and gravitational self-interaction |author=Sargent, C.; Deur, A.; Terzic, B. |journal=Physica Scripta |date=2024 |volume=99 |issue=7 |doi=10.1088/1402-4896/ad570f |arxiv=2301.10861|bibcode=2024PhyS...99g5043S }}</ref>
* The [[cosmic coincidence problem]], that is the fact that at present time, the purported repulsion of dark energy nearly exactly cancels the action of gravity in the [[Expansion of the universe|overall dynamics of the universe]].<ref name="Deur16a" />

Finally, the model made a prediction that the amount of missing mass (i.e., the dark mass in dark matter approaches) in elliptical galaxies correlates with the ellipticity of the galaxies.<ref name="Deur09" /> This was tested and verified.<ref>{{cite journal | last=Deur | first=A. | title=A relation between the dark mass of elliptical galaxies and their shape | journal=Mon. Not. R. Astron. Soc. | year=2014 | volume=438 | issue=2 | pages=1535–1551 | doi=10.1093/mnras/stt2293 | doi-access=free | arxiv=1304.6932 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal | last=Winters | first=D. | author2=Deur, A. | author3=Zheng, X. | title=Updated analysis of an unexpected correlation between dark matter and galactic ellipticity | journal=Mon. Not. R. Astron. Soc. | year=2022 | volume=518 | issue=2 | pages=2845–2852 | doi=10.1093/mnras/stac3236 | doi-access=free | arxiv=2207.02945 | bibcode=2023MNRAS.518.2845W }}</ref>

== Testing of alternatives to general relativity ==
{{Main|Tests of general relativity}}

Any putative alternative to general relativity would need to meet a variety of tests for it to become accepted.  For in-depth coverage of these tests, see Misner et al.<ref name=Misner1973 /> Ch.39, Will<ref name=Will1981 /> Table 2.1, and Ni.<ref name=Ni1972 />  Most such tests can be categorized as in the following subsections.

=== Self-consistency ===
Self-consistency among non-metric theories includes eliminating theories allowing [[tachyon]]s, ghost poles and higher order poles, and those that have problems with behaviour at infinity. Among metric theories, self-consistency is best illustrated by describing several theories that fail this test. The classic example is the spin-two field theory of Fierz and Pauli;<ref name=Fierz1939 /> the field equations imply that gravitating bodies move in straight lines, whereas the equations of motion insist that gravity deflects bodies away from straight line motion. Yilmaz (1971)<ref name=Yilmaz1973 /> contains a tensor gravitational field used to construct a metric; it is mathematically inconsistent because the functional dependence of the metric on the tensor field is not well defined.

=== Completeness ===
To be complete, a theory of gravity must be capable of analysing the outcome of every experiment of interest. It must therefore mesh with electromagnetism and all other physics. For instance, any theory that cannot predict from first principles the movement of planets or the behaviour of atomic clocks is incomplete.

Many early theories are incomplete in that it is unclear whether the density <math>\rho</math> used by the theory should be calculated from the stress–energy tensor <math>T</math> as <math>\rho=T_{\mu\nu}u^\mu u^\nu</math> or as <math>\rho=T_{\mu\nu}\delta^{\mu \nu}</math>, where <math>u</math> is the [[four-velocity]], and <math>\delta</math> is the [[Kronecker delta]]. The theories of Thirry (1948) and Jordan<ref name=Jordan1955 /> are incomplete unless Jordan's parameter <math>\eta\;</math> is set to -1, in which case they match the theory of Brans–Dicke<ref name=Brans1961 /> and so are worthy of further consideration. Milne<ref name=Milne1948 /> is incomplete because it makes no gravitational red-shift prediction. The theories of Whitrow and Morduch,<ref name=Whitrow1960 /><ref name=Whitrow1965 /> Kustaanheimo<ref name=Kustaanheimo1966 /> and Kustaanheimo and Nuotio<ref name=Kustaanheimo1967 /> are either incomplete or inconsistent. The incorporation of Maxwell's equations is incomplete unless it is assumed that they are imposed on the flat background space-time, and when that is done they are inconsistent, because they predict zero gravitational redshift when the wave version of light (Maxwell theory) is used, and nonzero redshift when the particle version (photon) is used. Another more obvious example is Newtonian gravity with Maxwell's equations; light as photons is deflected by gravitational fields (by half that of general relativity) but light as waves is not.

=== Classical tests ===
{{Main|Tests of general relativity}}
There are three "classical" tests (dating back to the 1910s or earlier) of the ability of gravity theories to handle relativistic effects; they are [[gravitational redshift]], [[gravitational lensing]] (generally tested around the Sun), and anomalous perihelion advance of the planets. Each theory should reproduce the observed results in these areas, which have to date always aligned with the predictions of general relativity. In 1964, [[Irwin I. Shapiro]] found a fourth test, called the [[Shapiro delay]]. It is usually regarded as a "classical" test as well.

=== Agreement with Newtonian mechanics and special relativity ===
As an example of disagreement with Newtonian experiments, Birkhoff<ref name=Birkhoff1943>{{cite journal | last1 = Birkhoff | first1 = G. D. | year = 1943 | title = Matter, electricity and gravitation in flat space-time | journal =   Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences| volume = 29 | issue = 8| pages = 231–239 | doi=10.1073/pnas.29.8.231| pmid = 16578082 |bibcode = 1943PNAS...29..231B | pmc = 1078600| doi-access = free }}</ref> theory predicts relativistic effects fairly reliably but demands that sound waves travel at the speed of light. This was the consequence of an assumption made to simplify handling the collision of masses.{{citation needed|date=August 2015}}

=== The Einstein equivalence principle ===
{{Main|Equivalence principle}}

Einstein's Equivalence Principle has three components. The first is the uniqueness of free fall, also known as the Weak Equivalence Principle. This is satisfied if inertial mass is equal to gravitational mass. ''η'' is a parameter used to test the maximum allowable violation of the Weak Equivalence Principle. The first tests of the Weak Equivalence Principle were done by Eötvös before 1900 and limited ''η'' to less than 5{{e|-9}}. Modern tests have reduced that to less than 5{{e|-13}}. The second is Lorentz invariance. In the absence of gravitational effects the speed of light is constant. The test parameter for this is ''δ''. The first tests of Lorentz invariance were done by Michelson and Morley before 1890 and limited ''δ'' to less than 5{{e|-3}}. Modern tests have reduced this to less than 1{{e|-21}}. The third is local position invariance, which includes spatial and temporal invariance. The outcome of any local non-gravitational experiment is independent of where and when it is performed. Spatial local position invariance is tested using gravitational redshift measurements. The test parameter for this is ''α''. Upper limits on this found by Pound and Rebka in 1960 limited ''α'' to less than 0.1. Modern tests have reduced this to less than 1{{e|-4}}.<ref name=WillReview2014 />

[[Leonard I. Schiff|Schiff]]'s conjecture states that any complete, self-consistent theory of gravity that embodies the Weak Equivalence Principle necessarily embodies Einstein's Equivalence Principle. This is likely to be true if the theory has full energy conservation. Metric theories satisfy the Einstein Equivalence Principle. Extremely few non-metric theories satisfy this. For example, the non-metric theory of Belinfante & Swihart<ref name=Belinfante1957a /><ref name=Belinfante1957b /> is eliminated by the ''THεμ'' formalism for testing Einstein's Equivalence Principle.  Gauge theory gravity is a notable exception, where the strong equivalence principle is essentially the [[minimal coupling]] of the [[gauge covariant derivative]].

=== Parametric post-Newtonian formalism ===
{{Main|Parameterized post-Newtonian formalism}}

See also [[Tests of general relativity]], Misner et al.<ref name=Misner1973 /> and Will<ref name=Will1981 /> for more information.

Work on developing a standardized rather than ad hoc set of tests for evaluating alternative gravitation models began with Eddington in 1922 and resulted in a standard set of Parametric post-Newtonian numbers in Nordtvedt and Will<ref name=Nordtvedt1972>{{cite journal | last1 = Nordtvedt Jr | first1 = K. | last2 = Will | first2 = C. M. | year = 1972 | title = Conservation laws and preferred frames in relativistic gravity II | journal = The Astrophysical Journal | volume = 177 | page = 775 | bibcode = 1972ApJ...177..775N | doi = 10.1086/151755 | doi-access = free }}</ref> and Will and Nordtvedt.<ref name=Will1972 /> Each parameter measures a different aspect of how much a theory departs from Newtonian gravity. Because we are talking about deviation from Newtonian theory here, these only measure weak-field effects. The effects of strong gravitational fields are examined later.

These ten are: <math>\gamma, \beta,\eta,\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3,\zeta_1,\zeta_2,\zeta_3,\zeta_4.</math>

*<math>\gamma</math> is a measure of space curvature, being zero for Newtonian gravity and one for general relativity.
*<math>\beta</math> is a measure of nonlinearity in the addition of gravitational fields, one for general relativity.
*<math>\eta</math> is a check for preferred location effects.
*<math>\alpha_1,\alpha_2,\alpha_3</math> measure the extent and nature of "preferred-frame effects". Any theory of gravity in which at least one of the three is nonzero is called a preferred-frame theory.
*<math>\zeta_1,\zeta_2,\zeta_3,\zeta_4,\alpha_3</math> measure the extent and nature of breakdowns in global conservation laws. A theory of gravity possesses 4 conservation laws for energy-momentum and 6 for angular momentum only if all five are zero.

=== Strong gravity and gravitational waves ===
{{Main|Tests of general relativity}}

Parametric post-Newtonian is only a measure of weak field effects. Strong gravity effects can be seen in compact objects such as [[white dwarf]]s, [[neutron star]]s, and black holes. Experimental tests such as the stability of white dwarfs, spin-down rate of [[pulsar]]s, orbits of [[binary pulsar]]s and the existence of a black hole horizon can be used as tests of alternative to general relativity. General relativity predicts that gravitational waves travel at the speed of light. Many alternatives to general relativity say that gravitational waves travel faster than light, possibly breaking causality. After the multi-messaging detection of the [[GW170817]] coalescence of neutron stars, where light and gravitational waves were measured to travel at the same speed with an error of 1/10<sup>15</sup>, many of those modified theories of gravity were excluded.

=== Cosmological tests ===
Useful cosmological scale tests are just beginning to become available.<ref name=WillReview2014 />{{rp|88}} Given the limited astronomical data and the complexity of the theories, comparisons involve complex parameters. For example, Reyes et al.,<ref>{{cite journal | last1=Reyes | first1=Reinabelle | last2=Mandelbaum | first2=Rachel | last3=Seljak | first3=Uros | last4=Baldauf | first4=Tobias | last5=Gunn | first5=James E. | last6=Lombriser | first6=Lucas | last7=Smith | first7=Robert E. | title=Confirmation of general relativity on large scales from weak lensing and galaxy velocities | journal=Nature | publisher=Springer Science and Business Media LLC | volume=464 | issue=7286 | year=2010 | issn=0028-0836 | doi=10.1038/nature08857 | pages=256–258| pmid=20220843 |arxiv=1003.2185| bibcode=2010Natur.464..256R | s2cid=205219902 }}</ref> analyzed 70,205 [[Luminous infrared galaxy|luminous red galaxies]] with a cross-correlation involving galaxy velocity estimates and gravitational potentials estimated from lensing and yet results are still tentative.<ref name="Clifton"/>{{rp|164}}

For those theories that aim to replace dark matter, observations like the [[galaxy rotation curve]], the [[Tully–Fisher relation]], the faster velocity dispersions of [[dwarf galaxies]], and the [[gravitational lens]]ing due to galactic clusters act as constraints. For those theories that aim to replace [[Cosmic inflation|inflation]], the size of ripples in the spectrum of the [[cosmic microwave background radiation]] is the strictest test. For those theories that incorporate or aim to replace dark energy, the supernova brightness results and the age of the universe can be used as tests. Another test is the flatness of the universe. With general relativity, the combination of baryonic matter, dark matter and dark energy add up to make the universe exactly flat.

== Results of testing theories ==

=== Parametric post-Newtonian parameters for a range of theories ===
(See Will<ref name=Will1981 /> and Ni<ref name=Ni1972 /> for more details. Misner et al.<ref name=Misner1973 /> gives a table for translating parameters from the notation of Ni to that of Will)

General Relativity is now more than 100 years old, during which one alternative theory of gravity after another has failed to agree with ever more accurate observations. All experimental tests agree with general relativity so far, and so Parametric post-Newtonian analysis immediately eliminates all the scalar field theories in the table. A full list of Parametric post-Newtonian parameters is not available for Whitehead,<ref name=Whitehead1922 /> Deser-Laurent,<ref name=Deser1968 /> Bollini–Giambiagi–Tiomino,<ref name=Bollini1970 /> but in these three cases <math>\beta=\xi</math>,{{Citation needed|date=January 2019}} which is in strong conflict with general relativity and experimental results. In particular, these theories predict incorrect amplitudes for the Earth's tides. A minor modification of [[Whitehead's theory of gravitation|Whitehead's theory]] avoids this problem.  However, the modification predicts the [[Nordtvedt effect]], which has been experimentally constrained.{{Citation needed|date=March 2025}}

=== Theories that fail other tests ===
The stratified theories of Ni,<ref name=Ni1973 /> Lee Lightman and Ni<ref name=Lee1974 /> are non-starters because they all fail to explain the perihelion advance of Mercury. The bimetric theories of Lightman and Lee,<ref name=Lightman1973 /> Rosen,<ref name=Rosen1975 /> Rastall<ref name=Rastall1979 /> all fail some of the tests associated with strong gravitational fields. The scalar–tensor theories include general relativity as a special case, but only agree with the Parametric post-Newtonian values of general relativity when they are equal to general relativity to within experimental error. As experimental tests get more accurate, the deviation of the scalar–tensor theories from general relativity is being squashed to zero. The same is true of vector–tensor theories, the deviation of the vector–tensor theories from general relativity is being squashed to zero. Further, vector–tensor theories are semi-conservative; they have a nonzero value for <math>\alpha_2</math> which can have a measurable effect on the Earth's tides. Non-metric theories, such as Belinfante and Swihart,<ref name=Belinfante1957a /><ref name=Belinfante1957b /> usually fail to agree with experimental tests of Einstein's equivalence principle. And that leaves, as a likely valid alternative to general relativity, nothing except possibly Cartan.<ref name=Cartan1922 /> That was the situation until cosmological discoveries pushed the development of modern alternatives.
